keyword: how do astronauts go to the bathroom in space
claims: Astronauts use specialized vacuum toilets in space that rely on airflow instead of gravity to collect waste.
A suction hose with a funnel is used for urination.
A seat with strong suction collects solid waste.
Solid waste is stored in containers for disposal or returning it to Earth.
The toilet system keeps waste from floating away.
The Waste and Hygiene Compartment (WHC) on the International Space Station (ISS) is a private stall where astronauts use a combination of hoses and a seat.
Astronauts use a hose with a specialized funnel to urinate, which can be used sitting or standing.
Urine is pulled away by airflow.
Astronauts sit on a small seat with a vacuum-powered, canister-based system for defecation to prevent waste from escaping.
Foot restraints and handholds keep astronauts securely in place in microgravity.
Urine on the International Space Station is collected and processed through a Urine Processor Assembly (UPA).
The UPA recycles urine into clean, drinkable water.
Feces are collected in bags, vacuum-sealed, and eventually stored before being burned up upon re-entry into the atmosphere.
The Universal Waste Management System (UWMS) is used on the ISS and Artemis missions.
The toilet area on the ISS is located in a private, enclosed node.
Air is constantly drawn into the toilet system when in use to prevent odor.
The system is designed to allow both urine and feces to be collected simultaneously for the female anatomy.
The European Space Agency (ESA) published a 52-second YouTube video titled 'International Space Station toilet tour' on May 8, 2015.
